I was looking for an apartment/house to rent in Santo Domingo. Someone advised Airnbn. Quick note here, I never plan my trips 2 days or more ahead of the travel, and I was expecting similar experience as I have from hotel booking websites. Here are the cons (I couldn't think of any pros): 1. The system is excessively hard on those who want to rent: - the registration is weird and unreasonable. Besides normal requirements (which you need to fulfil on normal hotel booking websites) they require you to attach a copy of your ID, at least two online IDs (ex Fb, gmail), photo. In my opinion since Airnbn is a sort of a booking system, it should have similar requirements to any hotel booking system and no more. The guests PAY upfront, why do they come up with the really heavy excessive verification system? If they are afraid of guests stealing or damaging the properties, this can happen in any hotel, but hotel booking systems nevertheless don't have those stupid verification requirements. - When I was trying to get through verification of online ID (FB, Gmail, etc) the system (on my mobile) kept returning me to the verification page after I logged in to FB from Airnbn without any information for me. So I was stuck on that step. Same with Gmail. When I stopped the app and relaunched it, after signing in to FB Airnbn would tell me that my account has already beed authorised but the system would again return me to the online ID verification page. Then I tried to go through the online ID verification on computer. And as I tried to do it, the system kept telling me that I am not using FB or Gmail often enough for it to be used for verification. However I use FB and GMAIL EVERY DAY for a few years! In fact due to this problem, the host of one of my bookings canceled my booking, saying that I didn't go through all the verification process. 2. Filtering -The filter is not complete, you cannot really limit the properties shown by specific area, amenities, use of the property (party or family for example) and many other things. 3. Representativeness - some listings have a couple or even one only image. So there is no system to require hosts to post certain number of images. 4. Inadequate system of contacting the host. Airnbnb doesn't allow phone communication with the host, you cannot get the host's telephone number before booking as well as after. If you make a message inquiry to host, it usually takes a few days before the hosts reply to you. Same about booking, many times you would do it just to know that later it will be canceled. 5. Some hosts are real stupid. I made a booking which was 100% confirmed. But then the host contacted me and asked me for address, and also why my phone was not accepting the call (I registered airnbn with my US number, and I was traveling in Dominican Republic, so it could be the reason of no calls coming through). But the host went real crazy about the registered in Airnbnb telephone not answering. Also, since the host asked me for address he didn't specify what kind of address he wanted (current, permanent, billing or what). So I gave him my residence address. And later he freaked out and reached me and said the address was wrong because my credit card is registered with another address. + my registered in Airbnb phone didn't accept his calls + I was stuck with that freaking online ID verification step, so he canceled the complete booking, which was evening and caused me tremendous number of problems. 6. Airnbn customer service is a joke. I was contacted by their customer service but I had to make an urgent call, so I asked them to call me back after 5 minutes. They tried to call me back 2 hours! later at 20:30 my time when I was resting. 7. Airnbn is discriminarory about guests vs hosts. I already mentioned that before. + the host can always do anything he wants with your reservation including cancelling it with no actual reason. While it takes so much effort for a guest to book anything! I hope this system disappears from Appstore, as I see so many negative comments here, but the freaking Airnbn doesn't seem to care and are not improving anything.

This happened because said lady had several houses and flats on their site, disguising her profession behind the shared private landlord facade of the site. With the full aprocal of Airbnb. But the fact remains that I, after having tried to get the lady to swap, had to cancel, and got another 25 % on top of the least 50 % of my deposit. I should have had a full refund. And a huge excuse. Probably even tort, as Airbnb should carry the warranty for directing its users to the correct place of booking. But especially the cover up (I know I never booked that place, the style and outline was completely wrong for my family and I) and the being tricked into believing we are all private people here, and Airbnb just accomodating services, really got me. This is close to a scam, and the marketing of Airbnb is probably unlawful, but at the very least not informing correctly. And how do I know Fanny is a professional? She also approached me with an offer outside of Airbnb for a consecutive week through her letting agency in France. At reduced price.

Ok, so there's definitely a massive bias of reviews in general towards negativity. People rarely make the effort to report that the service or product they purchased met their expectations. I guess that's not a story worth telling! I almost never right reviews or contribute to online forums, but I was so surprised with the amount of negative reviews on here about Airbnb I had to get involved, my entire motivation is to help reassure anyone who is considering using Airbnb. I have never hosted via the site, but have been a guest at a wide range of properties on over 30 occasions on 3 different continents. My feedback is really simple; I have never, ever, had anything but perfect experiences using this site. Every property I have stayed at has met or exceeded my expectations. Every host has been helpful, professional and accommodating. Every booking process has been easy, fast and trouble free. Best of all, I have had wonderful stays in great properties countless times for normally less than the price of an average, local, characterless hotel room. Having never had a problem, I can't comment on Airbnb's customer service as I've never needed it, and having never hosted, I can't comment on the hosting experience other than to say that practically every host I have had contact with has been overtly positive about their experiences. I recommend airbnb to everyone I know (and am staying in an airbnb place in Cape Town right now!). If you are considering using the site as a guest but have apprehensions, book a place for just a night or two and then extend if you're happy with it. I don't want to dismiss the bad experiences people on here are reporting. I'm sure they're all valid, but I am very confident they are an absolute minority of airbnb experiences, and probably a smaller % than dissatisfied hotel guests around the world! I also can't resist taking a dig at the people reporting that they paid crazy sums of money (thousands of USD per night!). In my view, no accommodation in the world is worth that much! Even if I was a millionaire, I can't imagine ever paying that kind of money for a nights accommodation and feeling that it was good value! I urge you to try Airbnb. You won't look back.

I recently rented a place in Toorak Australia. $5,000 a week. I know...it's a lot and I most likely won't get much sympathy but I am writing so the rest of you don't get scammed. Pulled up in a taxi and the driver said we were not in Toorak, Toorak was 20 minutes away. We went in and stayed the night as it was late. The next day I noticed the mail of the house. The address was not Toorak but a neighboring town. I contacted the owner and Airbnb. The owner stated I was wrong and Airbnb said they would look into it. An hour or so later Airbnb called me and said the owner was canceling the stay. I would be receiving a full refund and they would help me find a new place. I got an email stating a full refund. Yes, an email from Airbnb stating $5,000 would be back in my account in a few days. End of story right? Nope. The next day Airbnb contacts me and asks if I want to cancel the reservation. I ask why when I have already moved out per the owners request. I leave it at that and check into a hotel. The owner then contacts me and tells me he has spoken with the police and has filed a fraud charge against me. Not knowing what to do I get a local attorney who was extremely helpful. Apparently Airbnb in Australia is full of scams. Shortly after, Airbnb contacts me and says there will be no refund. After 3-4 calls the customer service person states "I am looking on a map and it looks close enough to me". I ask why the zip codes are different and how does a 20 minute drive constitute the same neighborhood? What about the email stating a refund? The answer was "you can file a complaint". So I did with documents supporting the discrepancies from the Australian government. I report it to Chase and decide to let it go as it will further ruin the vacation. The owner has since reduced his rates by over 50% and changed the address but is still part of Airbnb. Not a word from Airbnb. I filed a claim with the BBB in SF, the police in Australia said they have endless complaint with Airbnb. Buyer beware, it anything goes wrong Airbnb looks out for Airbnb. $5,000 gone and another $2,000 to an attorney. When a company doesn't even do a basic background check buyer beware.

Airbnb has done an excellent PR campaign in the UK over the last few months, making it sound so great as a concept. And to be fair I do know a couple of people who have made successful and happy bookings with them. BUT from my own pretty dire first experience I would only recommend using this site whilst exercising extreme caution and a healthy dose of scepticism. We were looking for an apartment in Palma de Mallorca for a few days ... One property clearly had incorrect information on the listing - ie, the title stated, and pictures showed, that it was a large 5 bed villa in what looked like an out-of-town location, BUT the 'blurb' underneath then went on to say that it was an apartment with only 2 bedrooms and was in the centre of town. I clicked on the 'Contact host' button rather than the 'Request to book' button, since I wasn't requesting to book, I simply wanted to clarify the issue re. the listing and give them the benefit of the doubt that it was a one-off mistake. However, in my private Airbnb messages, I just got an automated reply saying ‘Declined’ (thereby suggesting to other hosts who care to look that I’m somehow an undesirable tenant). How can a booking be “declined” when it was never requested in the first place?? If they meant that my request for information was “declined” that’s kinda even worse. It left a sour taste, ie, no personal response from the host explaining why the listing was wrong which it very, very clearly was… Another couple of listings we looked at – showing on the Airbnb map as being separate properties, a mile apart, and listed at different prices - both had exactly the same pictures!! Again no response to my polite request for clarification. A fourth property we were interested in looked like a big villa in a beachside location …. The response to the enquiry via the Airbnb message system requested my husband to contact the supposed host’s “wife” via another email address … this is a scam, which I acknowledge is absolutely not Airbnb’s fault. I got an automated email from Airbnb about 20 hrs later saying that they had detected a potential fraud and not to contact the host again. Which is good on the one hand that their systems spotted this, but bad in that in we had come up against a scam on their website in such a very short time, a property that didn’t exist for rent. And when I checked, the property was still being advertised on Airbnb four days AFTER they’d confirmed that it was a fraud!! The upshot is that, honestly, you cannot completely trust the listings. Remember that despite all the PR guff about “community” and “the sharing economy” – all cleverly designed to make us, the punters, think we’re part of something bigger and more noble than mere commerce - Airbnb is nothing more than an advertising platform and not a very reliable one at that. There are no guarantees, almost no customer service apart from automated emails, and Airbnb takes NO responsibility (as they do state in their terms and conditions, do read them before you book) for anything that goes wrong. Be fully aware that Airbnb does NOT vet or authenticate the properties offered, despite all the supposed ‘verification’ labels on the listings. If you discover a dubious listing before you actually book, there is no way to warn other users, as you cannot post a review or comment on Airbnb without paying for and staying in a property first. And if the property is not as advertised when you arrive and you decide not to stay, it will be counted as a cancellation by Airbnb and you will still not be permitted to post a review. So when you look at reviews, bear in mind that there may have been dissatisfied customers as well as happy ones, but they simply weren’t allowed to post their views. Just take huge care when using this site is all I’m saying, and NEVER book a place or fork out any cash without communicating directly, preferably several times, with the host beforehand, ensuring that all your queries have been answered. There are clearly lots of genuine hosts and great value to be had, but the increasing popularity of Airbnb has inevitably opened it up to many, many commercial agents looking to flog their inventory (rather than individual property owners trying to make a bit of extra cash from their much-loved home, which is what the site tries to convince you it is about) as well as outright scammers and charlatans. It all smacks of a business idea that was great when it started, but has grown too quickly to be able to keep up with even basic security and customer service considerations. You may get lucky and have a lovely time with Airbnb, but at least consider the potential pitfalls, of which there are many, and go into it with your eyes very wide open.

I personally have had no problems with AirBnb as far as how the site works technically. I have both hosted and been a guest. I'm a pretty active user. I started out thinking, this is the coolest idea ever! But since I've stayed and hosted a number of times, I have a little more perspective. I still have had no BAD experiences, just some stays better than others, so I've learned to be a little more discerning about what I want. And to not just rent the cheapest place just to brag on how much I saved over a hotel. We hosted for a year or so, but gave it up because, first we didn't really need the money, it was just a way to prompt us to take better care of the house and to meet new friends. But after a while, we realized our house wasn't ideal for it, and it was a lot of work. Hosts put a lot of effort into getting the house clean and ready for guests, at least we did. It was kinda fun, but also kinda a lot of work, and we also realized the guests weren't that interested in being our new best friends, they just wanted a cheap alternative to a hotel. My wife was pretty happy for me to delist our place. As a guest the places I've rented where I have my own run of the place, I've loved. When I really have been honest, the places where I am renting a bedroom and sharing everything else, not so much. Maybe it's just me, but I came to realize, that unless the host goes to great pains to make me at ease sitting in their easy chair in their living room, or digging around in their kitchen cabinets hunting for coffee, then I'm not "at ease". Instead, I feel a little uncomfortable invading someone else's space. If it's a single person, it seems OK, we're roomies for a short period. When it's a couple or a family, I very easily feel like "Gor-DON", the weird guy from the phone commercial. A couple has a private dynamic, even more so with a family. Realizing that without an invitation, I didn't feel comfortable in the common areas, I would find myself squirreled away in my little room in an otherwise comfortable house, wondering, why didn't I just rent a hotel room. About the third time this happened (I'm a slow learner), I finally said, why am I doing this, this is not fun, who am I kidding?. So now I only rent places where I get the whole place or it is somehow laid out to not make me feel like I'm the weird Uncle in the kid's bedroom. But then I find myself leaving a positive review whether I felt very welcomed or not, because I know they didn't intend to make me feel like an awkward 5th wheel, it's just how these things work out. If I were to leave negative feedback, I'm sure the host would be shocked, and say, gee, we had no idea you were unhappy. But this 'you know I don't feel comfortable in your house' conversation isn't something you want to start with your hosts when you're just going to be somewhere a couple of days. anyway, airbnb doesn't provide any kind of forum to discuss these kinds of things, so here it is. I started out thinking AirBnB was the greatest thing ever, but have since learned it is a little more delicate to be in someone else's place and feel comfortable. I'm still an active user, just a little more careful about which listings I'll book, and a little more honest with myself about when maybe a hotel is a better choice. And to all you hosts renting out the spare bedroom, with all those great pictures of Your easy chair in Your living room, and Your granite countertop in Your kitchen, please be aware that guests feel more than a little out of place in the middle of all that Youness unless you really go out of your way to make them welcome.

I'm using since a couple of months this platform as a host and experiences several trips. Here are my serious disappointments: #1 Don't rely on profiles, as a host you never really know who will come, many times people make a reservation for others. #2 As a guest the refund policy don't work in case the conditions are straight or moderate, even with medical certificate you will not see the funds back as you have to contact airbnb and they don't answer. I was planning on a month's stay in Boston, using Ahmed (an independent agent for owners' listing on bnb. This hospitality outsourcing business is becoming a cult for those inside the tent. The endless striving for Superhost status, the needy request for other hosts to give feedback on their listing, the 1000s of agonizing posts regarding the virtue of leaving of soap v tea bags, to iron sheets or not, supply shampoo or not, the cogitating about whether soap scum or drain hair, fridge access or feng shwui was the real cause of that last poor review.... Not to mention the thousands of horror stories and near misses that appear on the site's Group Host Anecdotes. These wanna be Martha Stewarts have created their own well furnished and tastefully decorated prisons. Hosts are hostage to guest reviews, and are developing coded review strategies to alert each other but not provoke the dreaded negative review, or worse apparently, no review. The supposed emphasis on security results in a "pants down bend over" protocol for hosts to "verify", but a loose protocol for guests who reportedly game the system. The site has inaccurate Google tags if you are searching for properties by location, a so called security device: but gives out real addresses to unverified guests whose emails are faked, whose phone numbers are no longer in service, who turn up with extra bodies, and who have trashed, burgled, and robbed hosts. And a hosting service who thinks is appropriate to use videos of sleeping women, (no sleeping men mind you) to advertise their site is just out of touch. These videos look real, and show women waking from sleep, apparently unaware they are being filmed. Airbnb say they are actors, but either way, it looks creepy. The site is hard work, glitchy, under resourced, slow to respond to issues, and lacking support for hosts. Forums do the works of site administrators, and newbies are tossed to the wolves. Guests have the whip hand, and hosts are just collateral damage. You may as well to do what they did in the old days, put up a sign: room for rent, apply within.

Airbnb is a wonderful company with great ideas. However, sometimes people can become frustrated especially when dealing with people across various time zones. Travel is a messy business. That being said, most of the problems come from the hosts, and not Airbnb itself. For example, my first experience with the company involved my host canceling just days before my arrival, based on the status on my age (Airbnb standards state you have to be 18+, however she wanted 21+)... Obviously I was frustrated. She had my money and wouldn't let me stay in her home. Airbnb quickly cleared the air, refunded me my money, and gave me 20% off plus an additional $100 for reparations and funds for my next booking. Often times its easy to blame the whole, when really it is simply the disorganization and miscommunication between host and guest. I encourage everyone to use Airbnb and support locals!

We emailed and received confirmation that the place was available for rent. We booked, no problem. Almost a month afterwards, we were cancelled due to the site double booking. I decided to try Airbnb.com for the first time for an upcoming trip to Boston because hotels were generally full for the conference I'll be attending. I was really happy to see that a ton of rentals near the conference center were available for my dates, were well reviewed, and were cheaper than the few remaining hotel options. I submitted my first formal rental request (with full payment) to a nearby apartment. The request expired after 24 hours because the person never bothered to respond. Same happened with the second request (now I had 2 holds for $1000+ each on my credit card and no reservation anywhere). I complained to airbnb and got a canned response that they encourage their property owners to respond promptly but that unfortunately some don't, and they recommend sending multiple informal requests to check availability instead of submitting a payment right away. OK... so I did that--I must have emailed a dozen rentals, all of which indicated they were available on my dates. One person responded saying it wasn't available. Another responded and tried to bait/switch me into a $450/night rental (I'd emailed about a $280/night rental). Everyone else blew me off. Sent another complaint to airbnb. Got the same canned response. I see many other people who've reviewed the site have had the same experience (or much worse)--I will not be using them. Ever.

Since its inception in 2008, Airbnb has faced a barrage of criticism, some quite troubling and some that has led to public battles. Following my own encounter with the company – and multiple failed attempts at extracting any kind of meaningful response from a perplexing labyrinth of customer service options – I am not in the least bit surprised. I have had 2 valid reservations cancelled by Airbnb by their automated robot system that claims to intercept what it views as inappropriate bookings, and my listing withdrawn both times. In the first instance, it took 5-6 weeks to reach a resolution. I am now entering my second week in the latest dispute and am not holding my breath. I am about to pull the plug on airbnb. Their competitors, especially Wimdu, are totally ahead of the game in customer service.

I've hosted 3 people so far. I have a small condo in a desirable area of Austin -- and it's my live/work space. I decided to try AirBnB to help pay my mortgage. I couch surf with family/friend while guests are here. The first guests were fine. The second left a URINE SOAKED MATTRESS (after also sending creepy texts asking to buy items out of my place). Yes, they got so drunk, they pissed the bed. Someone has a problem. AirBnB says they'll mediate disputes and that they have insurance, but their pretty pretty site doesn't provide details. After the guest refused to answer texts/calls/dispute resolution emails, AirBnB revealed to me that their insurance won't cover anything unless you have the original receipt. Because, you know, everyone saves the original receipt to their mattress, and the furniture they inherit, and everything. We are all that organized and life is perfect, right? Their insurance claim is baloney. I'm out $$$ to replace a mattress and buy waterproof covers for the new one. The third guests didn't damage the condo or anything, but while they said they were checking out at 9 am, they then proceeded to sit in my reserved parking spot until 7pm because they couldn't move their car because it had a breathalyzer on the ignition -- you know the kind where if you blow into it drunk, it prevents you from restarting the car for X number of hours? My apartment was fine, but having them camped out in their car for hours under my window was weird. My take away is that alcoholics and circuit party messes use AirBnB because it saves their credit cards getting dinged should they tear up a motel. Why AirBnB doesn't extend the same courtesy to hosts is beyond me, but their evasiveness on their website royally pisses me off. AirBnB will let you put a deposit on your unit -- as if you are a landlord contracting a lease. So I did it as a CYA and since then, I've gotten ZERO inquiries. Go figure.

What a great concept! I tried Airbnb for the first time when I flew to Seattle to visit my daughter at college. Every hotel I checked into was $150+ which I found to be too expensive just to lay my head at night! The home I chose to stay at had a wonderful and welcoming host who had many great ideas of things to do and places to go. I was able to come and go as I pleased, didn't have to pay for parking and no hotel fees/taxes to have to pay just a straight fee which was considerably less than a hotel. It was a wonderful experience and I can't wait until my next trip to use Airbnb again!

Our Booking with Airbnb (Confirmation Code: W3TCW3) was made in January, 2014 for an apartment in Izmir, Turkey which we paid for in full at that time (185.00 AUD - Receipt No: 2031616095). The apartment was advertised as "Deluxe Residence 1+1". On the day of check in (September 27, 2014), our hosts failed to meet us at the mutually agreed time at the apartment or provide any alternative arrangement. We phoned them at 11.30am to reconfirm our arrival time. We found that they were sleeping and our call had woken them. However, despite the language differences, we got the gist that they would be there to meet us in 10 minutes. As they hadn't arrived after 20 minutes, numerous other calls were made on our behalf by random helpful passers-by who spoke the local language. Despite all of their efforts, our hosts continued to let us down. A lady arrived at 1.30pm armed with towels and sheets and entered the building. A man on a bike appeared shortly after and also went inside. We followed them up the disgustingly dirty stairs to find the lady making a bed and the man talking on his phone. Neither of them were the owners and at no time did they attempt to communicate with us. We found the apartment to be filthy and smelling of cigarette smoke. The "well equipped kitchen" consisted of a rusting portable 2 burner electric cooktop with minimal cutlery, crockery and cooking utensils. We checked out the bathroom to find a broken toilet which wouldn't flush. We couldn't believe what we were seeing and took some photos (to the annoyance of the man who was still talking on his phone). By 1.55pm we had had enough of the constant lies and false promises from our hosts, so we went about finding alternate accommodation - this wasted most of our day, cost us money and was very stressful, particularly in a foreign country! After we finally found new accommodation, we cancelled the "Deluxe Residence 1+1" and promptly filed a report to Airbnb requesting a full refund due to extenuating circumstances. They advised us to take it up with our hosts first and said they would intervene if a solution could not be reached. We followed their instructions but we still haven't heard from our hosts to date (October 13) - Surprise, Surprise!! BUT we did receive a generic automated email response from Airbnb, dated September 28 (24 hours after we lodged our claim), saying "A refund is not available for this reservation, in accordance with the host's cancellation policy" and "If you have any questions, we have answers"!! What a cop out!! Since then we have tried to re-contact Airbnb's Help/Resolution Centre to no avail. Their website is poorly designed and has blatant non-working functions when you click on them, making it impossible for any further communication to take place. They don't even provide a contact phone number!! In summary, we have travelled the World extensively for years now and have never experienced such inefficiency and a lack of duty of care from any other booking Company. Airbnb's business ethics are appalling to say the least and they are a disgrace to the Travel Industry!! M and P Mason Australia

I used AirBnb with good experience, but the reservation process is awful because some hosts just do not answer at all or 3 weeks later. I am amazed about Airbnb just not put a very simple and clear policy about availability and time responding. It would be just a much better experience for everyone.

The first time I used AirBnB it was fine - we arranged a room at short notice and it all went smoothly. Since then I've tried multiple times and I've always been rejected by the hosts - despite having a positive rating. Hosts don't usually even provide a reason. I was hoping to use AirBnB instead of a hotel or hostel but that really doesn't work if it's unreliable.

all too often a hosts availability is not accurately reflected on their calender and I waste too much time waiting for approval only to be declined because they arent available or they just dont respond, also their instant book is not instant at all and also needs approval meanwhile I have over $500 on hold from my credit card waiting final authorisation for 10 days until its returned to me and until then thats $500 I am unable to spend

My hubby and I had our first Airbnb stay and everything went so smoothly. What an amazing idea and there are no worries with Airbnb's policies which protect both the host and the guest. Prior to this stay, I had a very nice host who had to cancel my reservation due to an overbooking and Airbnb quickly refunded my monies. Thank you Airbnb for such a wonderful way to travel without spending tons of money.

I love the idea of AirBnB but have not been able to contact the company to have a security deposit returned from one of my bookings. I contacted the owner of the house from whom I rented and he referred me back to AirBnB. Deceptive policy...

That's great to know you don't have to be surprised about the hotel prices every time you go on vacation. With Airbnb it's so easy to get your own temporary HOME all over the world. Easy navigation through website will help you to find a place of your dream, contact the host and pay it in one click.
Do it. You won't regret it.

We have used Airbnb twice this year and both times we were very pleased with our experience. I would recommend this site to anyone who would rather not pay the high rates hotels have with very little service.

We have used AirBnB 3 times already, all over the country (San Francisco, Chicago, and Nashville) and are signed up for a small apartment in Paris (can't wait). We have had a great experience, with all the places being as advertised and all the homeowners being very nice and helpful. Great idea! Louise Keim-Loesch
ARRIVED AND MONTSE WAS WAITING FOR US AT THE APT. THE APT HAD ALL WE NEEDED AND PLENTY OF BEDS.. LOCATION WAS PERFECT ... EVERYTHING WAS PERFECT!!
I had a great trip! My host was awesome.
Stay anywhere in the world with people you can trust, in unique properties. So much more personal than a hotel, feel like you live where you're staying.
I've never had a bad stay through Airbnb. I rely on other guest reviews to ensure my experience is going to be enjoyable. What a cool resource! Airbnb is the future of the hospitality industry.

Airbnb is more than just a low-cost vacation rentals website. It's the doorway to a whole new kind of community: One that shares homes and experience, befriends you, amazes you with the beauty of their hearts and living spaces, and literally lets you into their lives. If ever there was a more human and personal way to travel the world, meet interesting people, and learn from exhilarating experiences, I sure haven't heard of it. And here's the real kicker: You get all of this, for a steal of a deal! Infinitely better than looking out the window of a hotel room that looks exactly the same no matter which of a hundred countries you're in, and not knowing anyone in the area you're looking to explore.

I have had fantastic experiences staying with airbnb hosts outside of London, England and in Victoria, B.C., Canada. I love having locals to help me navigate a city that may be new to me, or help me find treasures I hadn't previously found on my own in previous visits. You meet some interesting and welcoming people along the way. I can't wait for my next journey and the airbnb hosts, new neighborhoods I might explore.

I stayed two nights in an airbnb house in Portland, ME. The room was fine, but now airbnb is requiring people to upload a copy of their driver's license to continue using it. That's nuts! These days, it's too easy for hackers to get into websites like airbnb. If that's what they're demanding now, then good-bye airbnb!
